candidate_relations.reason: Imaging shows a discrete solid retroareolar mass rather than diffuse adipose enlargement of pseudogynecomastia.
The new 1.5-cm lobulated subareolar solid structure lacks the mixed fat-and-glandular composition typical of hamartoma.
Mild tenderness occurs without fever, erythema, drainage, or a fluid collection to indicate subareolar abscess.
Adenosis is usually a microscopic lobular process in women and does not match this young man's discrete retroareolar papillomatous mass.
There is no trauma or surgery history and no calcified or oil-cyst imaging appearance of fat necrosis.
The small BIRADS III mass has no microcalcifications or malignant features, making ductal carcinoma in situ an incompatible malignant subtype.
Ultrasound describes a solid lobular structure rather than a fatty homogeneous lesion.
The lesion is only 1 to 1.5 cm, mildly tender, BIRADS III, and lacks suspicious calcification or invasive features.
The retroareolar mass has lobular solid architecture and is not characterized as fat on either ultrasound or mammography.
Mammography shows a lobulated soft-tissue mass without the encapsulated fat-and-fibroglandular mixture of a breast hamartoma.
A new small solid lobulated retroareolar mass beneath the nipple is the characteristic presentation of an intraductal papilloma in this case.
BIRADS III imaging without microcalcifications or invasive signs does not support labeling the papilloma as breast cancer.
Papilloma names the benign papillary tumor family but omits the intraductal location indicated by the retroareolar mass.
A 1.5-cm solid lobulated mass is a breast tumor, but this category does not distinguish the intraductal papilloma from malignant or stromal lesions.
Earlier ultrasound documented steroid-associated gynecomastia, but the current question concerns a new focal firm retroareolar mass after steroid cessation.
The focal retroareolar mass in a man is not the diffuse terminal-duct lobular proliferation represented by adenosis.
A breast adenoma is a distinct glandular tumor and does not specify the intraductal papillary origin of this subareolar lesion.
Fibroadenoma is uncommon in men and usually forms a mobile peripheral mass rather than a nipple-centered intraductal lesion.
Repeat ultrasound explicitly describes a solid structure, excluding a simple breast cyst.
A rapidly enlarging leaf-like phyllodes tumor is inconsistent with the small BIRADS III retroareolar papillomatous mass.
